meta.title: Who really said "The consumer isn't a moron; she is your wife"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: David Ogilvy, in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963). He wrote consumer, not customer — and the sentence does not stop where people stop quoting it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The consumer isn't a moron; she is your wife'?
meta.ogDescription: Ogilvy wrote it in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963) — though usually it is misquoted as "customer".

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
answer.sourceLine: Ogilvy wrote it in Confessions of an Advertising Man (Atheneum, 1963). Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ and the Wikipedia article devoted to the quotation ↗ both cite page 96 of the Ballantine printing. Twenty years later he used a slightly different wording in Ogilvy on Advertising.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 96 of the Ballantine printing, per Wikiquote and Wikipedia
Ogilvy on Advertising (1983), p. 170, per Wikiquote

source.excerpt: The consumer isn’t a moron; she is your wife. You insult her intelligence if you assume that a mere slogan and a few vapid adjectives will persuade her to buy anything. She wants all the information you can give her.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries this exact wording — isn’t, semicolon — with the two sentences that follow it, cited to Confessions of an Advertising Man, page 96 (Ballantine Books).
Wikipedia has an article on the quotation itself ↗, which cites the same book at the same page. It is filed under the popular wording, “The customer is not a moron” — which is not what Ogilvy wrote.

The same Wikiquote page ↗ records a second, later Ogilvy wording — “The consumer is not a moron, she is your wife” — citing Ogilvy on Advertising, page 170. Both are his; the 1963 book is the earlier of the two.
We searched Quote Investigator for this line and it has no article on it, so there is no specialist finding here to defer to or contradict.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗, citing Confessions of an Advertising Man, page 96 (Ballantine). We could not open the book — the Internet Archive’s scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition is lending-restricted — so the page number is Wikiquote’s and Wikipedia’s, not one we confirmed.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of David Ogilvy and the book’s publisher
source.rightsNote: Confessions of an Advertising Man was first published by Atheneum in August 1963 — well after 1931, the current cut-off for the United States public domain, so the book is still in copyright. Quoting one sentence with attribution is a different matter from reproducing the book.

author.name: David Ogilvy
author.heading: About David Ogilvy
author.metaLine: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
author.bio: David Mackenzie Ogilvy founded his advertising agency in New York in 1948 with $6,000 and financial backing from his brother Francis, then managing director of the London agency Mather & Crowther. By 1963 Ogilvy, Benson & Mather billed $55m across 19 clients, Rolls-Royce among them. Time called him “the most sought-after wizard in today’s advertising industry” in 1962, and he is widely called the father of advertising.

misattribution.heading: How it travels
misattribution.intro: The attribution is solid — this is Ogilvy, and nobody else has ever been credited with it. The wording is another matter: the version in circulation is not the one he wrote.

items.who: “The customer is not a moron. She’s your wife.”
items.why: This is the form the line is almost always quoted in, and it is the title Wikipedia files its article under ↗. Ogilvy wrote consumer, not customer. The swap is small and it moves the meaning: a consumer is a category an adman is addressing, a customer is someone already buying.

items.who: “The consumer is not a moron, she is your wife.”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ cites this form to Ogilvy on Advertising (1983), page 170. It is genuinely his — just twenty years later, and with a comma where the 1963 book has a semicolon.

The line is quoted as an aphorism and stops at wife. In the book it is the opening of an argument that ends She wants all the information you can give her — which is the practical instruction, and the part advertisers actually have to act on.

misattribution.truthLine: Ogilvy wrote it, in Confessions of an Advertising Man (1963) — as Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ records at page 96. The word is consumer.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the most-quoted sentence Ogilvy ever wrote, and it was aimed at his own industry. Wikipedia ↗ frames it as a response to the advertising of the early 1950s — loud, hectoring, exaggerated — and as an argument for a softer register that credits the reader with seeing through hype.

The gendering is period-specific and was noticed as such. In 1990 BBC Two broadcast a documentary on how the 1950s advertised to women and took its subtitle straight from the line: Washes Whiter: She’s Not a Moron — She’s Your Wife.
detailsBody: The sentence is regularly dated to 1955, eight years before the book. We could not establish that: Wikipedia makes the claim but sources it to a 2012 newspaper feature we were unable to reach from here, and we found no primary document — memo, speech or advertisement — carrying the line before Confessions of an Advertising Man. So this page dates it to the book, which is where it is demonstrably written down, and leaves the earlier date as an open question rather than an assertion.

A note on our sourcing: we could not open the book. The Internet Archive’s scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition is lending-restricted and not full-text searchable from here, so page 96 is Wikiquote’s and Wikipedia’s locator rather than one we checked.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section transcribes "The consumer isn't a moron; she is your wife. You insult her intelligence if you assume that a mere slogan and a few vapid adjectives will persuade her to buy anything. She wants all the information you can give her." and cites Confessions of an Advertising Man, p. 96 (Ballantine Books). The same page cites "The consumer is not a moron, she is your wife." to Ogilvy on Advertising, p. 170.

Wikipedia has an article titled "The customer is not a moron" about this quotation, attributing it to David Ogilvy, citing Confessions of an Advertising Man at page 96, describing it as a response to early-1950s advertising practice, and recording the 1990 BBC Two documentary "Washes Whiter: She's Not a Moron—She's Your Wife".
Wikipedia states Confessions of an Advertising Man was published by Atheneum in August 1963.
The Internet Archive holds a lending-restricted scan of the 1963 Atheneum edition of Confessions of an Advertising Man.
